Sic exspectatur iudicium — “Thus the judgment is awaited.” Apparently modeled on Cicero’s Argumentum orationis pro M. Tullio: “hoc iudicium sic exspectatur.”

Nette — Herbert Nette (1902–1994), journalist, editor, and writer. Nette, who also knew Ernst Jünger, met Carl Schmitt in the autumn of 1947 through Heinrich Gremmels. On 2 October 1947 he wrote to Schmitt asking for a meeting.
φθοραὶ τοίνυν ἐξ ἀνάγκης τότε μέγισται συμβαίνουσι τῶν τε ἄλλων ζῴων, καὶ δὴ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος ὀλίγον τι περιλείπεται: περὶ δὲ τούτους ἄλλα τε παθήματα πολλὰ καὶ θαυμαστά.

“The greatest destructions then necessarily occur among the other animals as well, and only a small remnant of the human race survives. And among these survivors many other strange and remarkable things then occur.”
Plato, Statesman, 270d; translation by Friedrich Schleiermacher.
ἐναντία — Movement in the opposite direction.
Baumgartner’s speech — The Bavarian politician Joseph Baumgartner (1904–1964) supported Bavarian independence.
qui accuse s’excuse — A reversal of the familiar saying qui s’excuse, s’accuse: “whoever excuses himself accuses himself.”
Hermann Hefele — (1885–1936), Romance-language scholar. Schmitt is referring to Hermann Hefele, Niccolo Machiavelli (Colemans kleine Biographien, 14), Lübeck 1933.
Kelsen’s presumption — See Hans Kelsen, Wer soll der Hüter der Verfassung sein?, Berlin 1931.
Kassner’s revealing remarks — Rudolf Kassner, “Faust oder der Barockmensch,” in Europäische Revue 18, 1942, pp. 199–213.

“Desire of power that ceaseth only in death” — “So that in the first place I put for a general inclination of all mankind a perpetual and restless desire of power after power, that ceaseth only in death.” Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, chapter 11.
To Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 213 ff., with slight differences.
Joy is an acceleration of the circulation of the blood — Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, chapter 6.
“as many pulsations as possible” — From Walter Pater’s 1868 essay “Poems by William Morris,” in Pre-Raphaelitism. A Collection of Critical Essays, edited by James Sambook, Chicago 1974, pp. 105–117.
Ed. Meyer — Schmitt is referring to Eduard Meyer, Caesars Monarchie und das Principat des Pompejus. Innere Geschichte Roms von 66 bis 44 v. Chr., Stuttgart/Berlin 1918.
James Burnham — J. Burnham, The Managerial Revolution: What Is Happening in the World, New York 1941, and later editions.
Max Stirner, p. 244 — Max Stirner, Der Einzige und sein Eigentum, Part II: “I,” chapter 4, “The Owner,” section A, “My Power.” Schmitt quotes the end of this chapter inaccurately.
Kaegi — Werner Kaegi, “Probleme des Rechtsstaats,” in Universitas 2, 1947, pp. 909–913.
Hobbes — Thomas Hobbes, “An Answer to Bishop Bramhall’s Book Called The Catching of the Leviathan,” in The English Works of Thomas Hobbes, edited by William Molesworth, vol. IV, p. 322.

“The animal, wholly immersed in time, perceives time just as little as the person wholly rapt in eternity. The perception of time can therefore belong only to man in his present amphibious existence—and even more strongly to Satan beneath him.”
Baader to Adolph Wagner, 10 September 1817, in Fr. von Baader, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 15, Leipzig 1857, p. 326.
Marie Stewens — (1899–1981), secondary-school teacher in Witten and sister-in-law of Peterheinrich Kirchhoff. See Schmittiana IV, 1994, pp. 272–284.

Robert Mohl — (1799–1875), professor of political science and politician. See Robert von Mohl, “Die Staatsromane. Ein Beitrag zur Literaturgeschichte der Staatswissenschaften,” in Zeitschrift für die gesamte Staatswissenschaft 2, 1845, pp. 24–74; and Geschichte der Staatswissenschaften, vol. 1, Erlangen 1855, Part III, pp. 167–214: “Staatsromane.”
Kleinwächter — Friedrich Kleinwächter, Die Staatsromane. Ein Beitrag zur Lehre vom Communismus und Socialismus, Vienna 1891.

Ernst Bloch — Schmitt is referring to Ernst Bloch, Freiheit und Ordnung. Abriss der Sozial-Utopien, New York 1946; later also included in E. Bloch, Das Prinzip Hoffnung, Frankfurt am Main 1959, pp. 547–729. See below, note to p. 234.
Thomas More, who invented the word “Utopia” — Thomas More, Libellus vere aureus nec minus salutaris quam festivus de optimo reipublicae statu, deque nova insula Utopia, Leuven 1516.
Pierre Linn — (1897–1966), French banker and philosopher, and an early translator of Schmitt into French, including Political Romanticism in 1928.
“Nothing is more to me than myself” — Final sentence of the introduction to Max Stirner, Der Einzige und sein Eigentum.
Veit — Otto Veit, “Die geistesgeschichtliche Situation des Naturrechts,” in Merkur, 1947, pp. 390–405.

Donoso Cortés had already understood this — See Juan Donoso Cortés, Über die Diktatur. Drei Reden aus den Jahren 1849/50, edited, translated from Spanish, and annotated by Günter Maschke, Vienna and elsewhere, 1996.
Letter from Popitz — Johannes Popitz wrote:

“[…] Above all, many thanks for sending me The Concept of the Political! We must talk about it. My impression is that you have achieved here the best thing I have yet read by you—and I have read a great deal that was excellent.”

“Donoso Cortés, tanned into table-leather and cut down into cheap novel-trim” — “Table-leather” is a malicious play on the name of Peter Tischleder (1891–1947), professor of Catholic moral theology and Christian social teaching in Münster, and from 1946 in Mainz. Schmitt regarded him as having a ponderous, “Tischleder-like” style. He was also the doctoral supervisor of Josef Westemeyer; see above, note to p. 11.

The writer Elisabeth Langgässer (1899–1950) discusses Donoso in the second book of her novel Das unauslöschliche Siegel (1946 and later editions). According to the Donoso specialist Günter Maschke, she treats him quite appropriately, contrary to Schmitt’s remark.
“the ascetic restraint of the scholarly academic” — Max Weber, Politik als Beruf, Munich/Leipzig 1919, p. 25. Schmitt used the second edition of 1926, which has identical pagination.

Winckelmann — Johannes Winckelmann (1900–1985), jurist and editor of Max Weber’s works, who had known Schmitt since 1938. See Stefan Breuer, “Klassiker der Karlsruher Republik. Johannes Winckelmann etabliert nach 1945 Max Weber,” in Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte IX, 2015, no. 2, pp. 89–104.
“spat out again by Leviathan three times” — See above, note to p. 7.
“the Russian major” — After Soviet troops captured Schlachtensee at the end of April 1945, Schmitt was questioned by a Russian officer.

Carl Tobias — An allusion to the apocryphal Old Testament Book of Tobit. Tobias is the son of a blind father whose sight is restored through him (Tobit 11). It is unclear who used the name as a pseudonym.
When the Roman Republic was in danger, the Senate declared a state of emergency and empowered the consuls with the formula:
Videant consules ne quid detrimenti res publica capiat.
“Let the consuls see to it that the state suffers no harm.”
The consuls then addressed the citizens with the words:
Qui rem publicam salvam esse velit, me sequatur.
“Whoever wishes the state to be saved, let him follow me.”
Altheim — Franz Altheim, Lex sacrata. Die Anfänge der plebeischen Organisation (Albae vigiliae, 1), Amsterdam 1940.
Plutarch — Plutarchi vitae parallelae. Recogn. Cl. Lindskog et K. Ziegler, vol. 3, fasc. 2, including the Lives of Galba and Otho and fragments of lost lives, 2nd ed., Leipzig 1973.
“If this night …” — See Max Weber, Politik als Beruf, Munich/Leipzig 1919, p. 66. Correct wording: “… has apparently blossomed so luxuriantly now.”
KDF — Kraft durch Freude (“Strength Through Joy”), the Nazi organization responsible for organizing leisure activities.
“Now there will …” — Max Weber, Politik als Beruf, Munich/Leipzig 1919, p. 56, not p. 57.
“Whoever wishes to act according to the ethics of the Gospel …” — Correctly:

“Whoever wishes to act according to the ethics of the Gospel should refrain from strikes—for they are coercion—and should join the yellow trade unions. Above all, however, he should not speak of ‘revolution.’ For that ethic surely does not mean to teach that civil war in particular is the only legitimate war.”
Max Weber, Politik als Beruf, Munich/Leipzig 1919, p. 55, not p. 57.
Hans Barth and his essay on Leviathan — H. Barth, “Wirklichkeit und Ideologie des totalen Staates,” in Neue Schweizer Rundschau NF 6, 1938, pp. 449–458.
Also: “Vom totalen Staat und seinen ideologischen Voraussetzungen,” in the same journal, pp. 614–627 and 673–682, including discussion of E. R. Huber.

Also: “Über die Entstehung der Ideologie vom totalen Staat,” in Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1938; reprinted in H. Barth, Denken in der Zeit. Philosophisch-politische Beiträge in der Neuen Zürcher Zeitung 1932–1964, with an introduction by Hermann Lübbe, Zurich 1988, pp. 200–209.
“the refined, righteous tone of the comb-makers” — See Gottfried Keller, Die drei gerechten Kammacher (“The Three Righteous Comb-Makers”).
Fritz Ernst in Corona VII — F. Ernst, “Johannes von Müller. Zürcher Rede,” in Corona 7, 1937, pp. 109–126; the quotation appears on p. 123.
Schmitt apparently saw a parallel with his own life in Müller’s decision to enter the service of Jérôme Napoléon, King of Westphalia, as a councillor of state.

Letter from Barion dated 11 November 1947 — The long letter, RW 265 no. 694/1, concerns Rudolph Sohm. Before turning to Sohm, Barion describes the difficulties he was having in being reinstated in his professorship at Bonn.
Aldous Huxley — In the epilogue to his book, Huxley explains the Shakespeare quotation from which the title of his novel comes. This is presumably what Schmitt means by “gloss.”
Annie Kraus — See below, note to p. 155.
Mr. Dr. R. — Possibly Eduard Rosenbaum.
Baader … answered prayer — Franz von Baader, Vorlesungen über religiöse Philosophie I/1, Munich 1827, pp. 87 ff.
Minima non curat praetor, maxima non curat praetor — “The praetor does not concern himself with small matters; the praetor does not concern himself with great matters either.”
The first sentence comes from Roman law. Schmitt added the second himself.

Kierkegaard, The Concept of Anxiety — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Søren Kierkegaard, Gesammelte Werke, with an afterword by Christoph Schrempf, translated by Wolfgang Pfleiderer and Christoph Schrempf, Part 5: Der Begriff der Angst, Jena 1912.
Chapter 3: “Anxiety as a Consequence of That Sin Which Consists in the Absence of Consciousness of Sin,” pp. 77–107; section 2: “Anxiety Dialectically Defined in Relation to Fate,” pp. 93–100.

Zeller — Schmitt is probably referring to Eduard Zeller, Geschichte der deutschen Philosophie seit Leibniz (= Geschichte der Wissenschaften in Deutschland, published by the Historical Commission of the Royal Academy of Sciences, 13), 2nd ed., Munich 1875.
